author: Ivan Svetunkov

questions.question: What data from the M5 competition were used in the empirical analysis, and how were they split for estimation and evaluation?
questions.answer: The M5 series were aggregated to monthly frequency and to department-store level to avoid intermittence, giving 70 series of 63 observations. They were grouped by department into seasonal and non-seasonal groups (classified by adam()); one group of a single series was removed, leaving 11 groups. Long histories: the first 51 observations for estimation and the last 12 held out. Short histories: the last 36 observations, 24 for estimation and the same last 12 held out.
questions.notes: Must give the aggregation, the 63 observations and both splits with the 12-observation holdout.
questions.marking: Required: the M5 series were aggregated to monthly frequency and to department-store level, giving series of 63 observations; long histories use the first 51 observations for estimation and hold out the last 12; short histories use the last 36 observations, 24 for estimation and the same last 12 held out. Not required: the purpose (avoiding intermittence), the 70 series, the grouping by department into seasonal and non-seasonal groups classified by adam(), the removal of a group of one series, the 11 groups. Wrong: a different aggregation, sample length, split or holdout.

questions.question: Which PIC restrictions did the automatic selection choose for the 11 VETS D models on the M5 data, and how often was each chosen?
questions.answer: PIC(LS,S,N) in 6 groups, PIC(L,L,N) in 2, and PIC(N,N,N), PIC(L,N,N) and PIC(LS,S,S) in 1 each. Only one (seasonal) group had common seasonal components.
questions.notes: Must give PIC(LS,S,N) as the most frequent, chosen in 6 of 11.
questions.marking: Required: PIC(LS,S,N) is the most frequent, chosen in 6 of the 11 groups. Not required: the other restrictions and counts (PIC(L,L,N) in 2; PIC(N,N,N), PIC(L,N,N) and PIC(LS,S,S) in 1 each), or that only one group had common seasonal components. Wrong: another restriction as the most frequent, or another count for PIC(LS,S,N).

questions.question: On the M5 data, which model had the lowest overall geometric mean and median rMAE (relative to Naïve forecasts), with long and with short histories?
questions.answer: VETS D on both measures and both lengths. Long: geometric mean 0.894 and median 0.934, against 0.906 and 0.960 for VETS F and at least 0.917 and 0.957 for the ETS models. Short: 0.936 and 0.974, against 1.011 and 1.000 for VETS F and at least 0.991 and 0.988 for the ETS models.
questions.notes: Must name VETS D for both lengths; this is over all series, not the seasonal or non-seasonal subsets.
questions.marking: Required: VETS D, for both long and short histories and on both the geometric mean and the median of rMAE over all series. Not required: the values. Wrong: another model for either history length or either measure; an answer taken from the seasonal or non-seasonal series alone instead of all series.

questions.question: What coverage did the 95% prediction intervals of each model reach on the long M5 histories (51 observations for estimation)?
questions.answer: Long histories: ETS LN 0.934, ETS (ADAM) 0.925, ETS 0.937, VETS D 0.947, VETS F 0.982. The three ETS models are below 95%; VETS F is a little too wide; VETS D is closest to 95%.
questions.notes: Must give the VETS D and VETS F values and say the ETS models fall short of 95%. Values for the short histories are not required and not wrong.
questions.marking: Required: VETS D 0.947 and VETS F 0.982, and that the three ETS models fall short of 95%. Also correct: the ETS values (ETS LN 0.934, ETS (ADAM) 0.925, ETS 0.937); VETS F is a little too wide; VETS D is closest to 95%. Not required: values for the short histories (not wrong either). Wrong: other values for the long histories.

questions.question: How were the data generated in the simulation experiment?
questions.answer: With sim.ves() from the legion package: VETS(A,N,A) data exponentiated to give VETS(M,N,M;LN), from each of the nine PIC variants studied. Quarterly seasonality (m = 4), 24 or 64 observations (6 or 16 years) with the last 8 held out, groups of 2, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 series, initial level from [4, 10], seasonal indices from (−1, 1) normalised, independent normal errors with standard deviation 0.3, smoothing parameters set by variant (α = 0.3 and γ = 0.1 for PIC(LS,*,*); α in [0, 0.3] and γ = 0.1 for PIC(S,*,*); α in [0, 0.3] and γ in [0, 1 − α] for PIC(N,*,*)), and 1000 iterations.
questions.notes: Must give the model, quarterly data, the two sample lengths and the group sizes.
questions.marking: Required: the model, VETS(M,N,M;LN) (VETS(A,N,A) data exponentiated); quarterly data; the two sample lengths, 24 and 64 observations; the group sizes 2, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 series. Not required: the generating function (sim.ves() from legion), the nine PIC variants used to generate data, the 8-observation holdout, the initial level and seasonal indices, the error standard deviation 0.3, the smoothing parameters, the 1000 iterations. Wrong: another model, frequency, sample length or group size.

questions.question: What does the model name VETS(M,Md,M;LN)PIC(LTSD,LTS,S) mean?
questions.answer: A pure multiplicative vector ETS model with a multiplicative damped trend and multiplicative seasonality, applied to log-transformed data (LN). PIC(LTSD,LTS,S): the smoothing parameters of level, trend and seasonality and the damping parameter are common to all series (P = LTSD); the initial level, trend and seasonal indices are common (I = LTS); and only the seasonal component is common, while level and trend are individual (C = S).
questions.notes: Must read each of P, I and C correctly. Accept 'damped trend' without 'multiplicative' for Md: the paper takes the letters from the ETS taxonomy without spelling out Md. If the answer gives the block matrices of Table 1, accept either the printed values (individual seasonal W_3 = Φ; common parameters A = α1'_n, B = β1'_n, Γ = γ1'_n) or the claimset's corrected ones (W_3 = I_n; A = αI_n, B = βI_n, Γ = γI_n).
questions.marking: Required: a correct reading of each of P, I and C: P = LTSD, the smoothing parameters of level, trend and seasonality and the damping parameter are common to all series; I = LTS, the initial level, trend and seasonal indices are common; C = S, only the seasonal component is common, while level and trend are individual. Also correct: 'damped trend' for Md, with or without 'multiplicative'. If the answer gives block matrices, both forms are correct: for an individual seasonal component W_3 = Φ or W_3 = I_n; for common smoothing parameters A = α1'_n or A = αI_n, B = β1'_n or B = βI_n, Γ = γ1'_n or Γ = γI_n. Not required: that the model is pure multiplicative on log-transformed data. Wrong: misreading any of P, I or C.

questions.question: In the space-planning evaluation on the M5 data (forecasts 3, 6 and 12 months ahead), at which of these horizons does either VETS model have the lowest GMRAE of the five models, with long and with short histories?
questions.answer: Long histories: at none; a univariate ETS model is lowest at every horizon (ETS (ADAM) 0.716 at 3 months, ETS 0.827 at 6 and 0.939 at 12). Short histories: at 3 months (VETS D 1.037) and 12 months (VETS F 0.872), but not at 6 months, where ETS (0.946) is lower than both VETS models. The authors say the VETS models do much better on short histories.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says a VETS model has the lowest GMRAE at every horizon on short histories, or at any horizon on long histories.
questions.marking: Required: long histories: at no horizon, a univariate ETS model is lowest at each of 3, 6 and 12 months; short histories: a VETS model is lowest at 3 months (VETS D) and 12 months (VETS F) but not at 6 months, where ETS is lowest. Not required: the values; that the authors say the VETS models do much better on short histories. Wrong (overreach): a VETS model lowest at every horizon on short histories, or at any horizon on long histories.

questions.question: On short M5 histories, are the prediction intervals of VETS D better than those of the univariate ETS models?
questions.answer: In coverage yes: 0.970 against 0.815–0.886 for the ETS models. In relative pinball no: VETS D has higher upper and lower pinball values than all three ETS models (e.g. upper 2.515). The authors therefore do not recommend VETS when the pinball measure matters most and the history is short.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says VETS D has better intervals without separating coverage and pinball.
questions.marking: Required: separates the two measures: in coverage yes (VETS D 0.970 against 0.815 to 0.886 for the ETS models); in relative pinball no (VETS D has higher upper and lower pinball values than all three ETS models). Not required: the values; that the authors do not recommend VETS when pinball matters most and the history is short. Wrong (overreach): saying VETS D has better intervals without separating coverage and pinball.

questions.question: In the MCB test on rMAE that the paper reports for the M5 data (its Figure 2), are the differences between the VETS and ETS models on the same history length (long with long, short with short) statistically significant?
questions.answer: No. VETS F on long histories has the lowest mean rank, but it is not significantly different from VETS D, ETS LN, ETS (ADAM) and ETS on long histories or from VETS D on short ones; on short histories the ETS models do worse in mean rank, but those differences are not significant either.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says VETS is significantly more accurate than ETS on the same history length. A right answer need not mention that VETS F has the lowest mean rank. Comparisons across lengths (Long VETS F against the short-history ETS models and Short VETS F) are significant in Figure 2; saying so is not overreach.
questions.marking: Required: no; within the same history length no difference between the VETS and ETS models is statistically significant. Also correct: comparisons across history lengths (long-history VETS F against the short-history ETS models and short-history VETS F) are significant. Not required: that VETS F on long histories has the lowest mean rank; that the ETS models have worse mean ranks on short histories. Wrong (overreach): saying VETS is significantly more accurate than ETS on the same history length.

questions.question: Do the paper's simulation and empirical results cover vector ETS models with a trend component?
questions.answer: No. The simulation uses only VETS(M,N,M;LN), and on the M5 data models with trend were excluded because the trends in the two trended series were weak. The authors name the trend element as something that may change how the methods behave, for future work.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer extends the findings to trended models.
questions.marking: Required: no; the results do not cover models with a trend. Not required: the reasons (the simulation uses only VETS(M,N,M;LN); on the M5 data trend models were excluded because the trends of the two trended series were weak); that the authors name the trend element for future work. Wrong (overreach): extending the findings to trended models.

questions.question: When do common seasonal components (PIC(*,S,S)) help forecast accuracy, and when do they harm it?
questions.answer: They help only when the series share very similar seasonal patterns. In the simulation they do well on data with common seasonal components, with moderate gains over PIC(N,N,N), though no better than common initial seasonal indices with individual components (PIC(*,S,N)). On data with individual seasonal components and initial values (the most flexible DGPs) they are much worse than the correct method in accuracy and do poorly in pinball values. The authors recommend them only for homogeneous series; on the M5 data they were chosen for only one of the 11 groups.
questions.notes: Must say they help only for series with very similar seasonal patterns and harm accuracy on data with individual seasonal components. Overreach if the answer says common seasonal components improve accuracy in general. Accept that they bring no gain over PIC(*,S,N) even on data with common seasonality (Section 5.3.1, Table 7; Section 5.3.2, the appendix table of pinball values by group size for the PIC(LS,S,S) DGP). The M5 frequency is not required.
questions.marking: Required: they help only for series with very similar seasonal patterns, and they harm accuracy on data with individual seasonal components (and individual initial values). Also correct: they bring no gain over common initial seasonal indices with individual components (PIC(*,S,N)), even on data with common seasonality; they give moderate gains over PIC(N,N,N) on data with common seasonal components; they do poorly in pinball values on the most flexible data. Not required: that on the M5 data they were chosen for only one of the 11 groups. Wrong (overreach): saying common seasonal components improve accuracy in general.

questions.question: What evidence supports the finding that common smoothing parameters improve forecasts, and what limitations of this evidence does the paper itself state?
questions.answer: In the simulation, within each block of methods the pinball values improve as smoothing parameters are made common (PIC(LS,*,*) better than PIC(S,*,*), better than PIC(N,*,*)) on data from every DGP, and rMAE improves slightly with them on data from PIC(LS,S,S). On the M5 data the selection chose common smoothing parameters for most groups, and the authors say the parameters, particularly for level and seasonality, benefited from common estimation. Limitations the authors state: on data generated with individual parameters (PIC(N,N,N)), restricting them lowers point accuracy, though not substantially; the simulated smoothing parameters cover a restricted range, not the whole parameter space; and additional seasonal indices and the trend element, not studied, may change how the methods behave.
questions.notes: Must give the simulation pinball result (common smoothing parameters lower pinball values within each block, on data from every DGP; Section 5.3.2) and at least one limitation stated in the paper or the claimset. Stated limitations: restricted smoothing parameters lower accuracy on PIC(N,N,N) data, though not substantially (Section 5.3.1); the simulated smoothing parameters do not cover the whole parameter space (Section 5.2); additional seasonal indices and the trend element may change how the methods behave (Section 7). The rMAE result and the M5 selection are not required. The overfitting explanation is the paper's claim, not a stated limitation; that it is untested is the claimset's open question O1, which counts as a claimset statement. Limits: the claimset's limitation objects are the authors' statements too, so a limit given from the claimset is not wrong. Correct: limits stated in the paper or the claimset, or 'none stated' where the paper states none. Wrong: a limit attributed to the paper that neither document states.
questions.marking: Required: the simulation result that, within each block of methods, making smoothing parameters common lowers pinball values (PIC(LS,*,*) better than PIC(S,*,*), better than PIC(N,*,*)) on data from every data generating process. Not required: that rMAE improves slightly with common parameters on data from PIC(LS,S,S); that the selection on the M5 data chose common smoothing parameters for most groups; any limitation. Acceptable limitations: on data generated with individual parameters (PIC(N,N,N)), restricting the smoothing parameters lowers point accuracy, though not substantially; the simulated smoothing parameters cover a restricted range, not the whole parameter space; the simulation covers only VETS(M,N,M;LN) on quarterly data; models with a trend are not analysed, and additional seasonal indices or the trend element may change how the methods behave; whether the restrictive variants work on histories as short as about one year is not known; groups of more than 50 series were not tested; whether common smoothing parameters reduce overfitting because they are averaged across series is not established. Limitations: correct if the answer gives limitations from this list or says the authors state none. Wrong: presenting as the authors' a limitation not in this list (also overreach).

questions.question: What evidence supports the claim that PIC(LS,S,N) is one of the most robust variants, and what limitations of this evidence does the paper itself state?
questions.answer: In the simulation the PIC(*,S,N) methods have rMAE close to that of the correct method on data from every DGP, being only slightly less accurate, and in pinball values they are robust compared with the other methods: worse than the correct method on the most flexible data, but less so than PIC(*,S,S), and better than the flexible methods on the most restrictive data. With 50 series of common seasonality, PIC(LS,S,N) has a 35% lower pinball value than PIC(N,N,N). On the M5 data it was the restriction chosen most often (6 of 11 groups), which the authors say validates the simulation finding. Limitations the authors state: the PIC(*,S,N) methods are outperformed by the flexible PIC(*,N,N) methods when the data favour those, so they suit series with similar seasonal patterns; and the simulated smoothing parameters cover a restricted range, not the whole parameter space.
questions.notes: Must give the simulation evidence (rMAE of PIC(*,S,N) close to the correct method across DGPs; Section 5.3.1), the M5 selection frequency (6 of 11; Table 13), and at least one limitation stated in the paper or the claimset. Stated limitations: outperformed by PIC(*,N,N) when the DGP favours those, so for series with similar seasonal patterns (Section 5.3.3); restricted range of smoothing parameters (Section 5.2). A right answer need not give the 35% figure. Wrong: saying PIC(*,S,N) has lower pinball values than every method but the correct one (Table 10 contradicts it). That the selection frequency does not itself measure robustness is the claimset's warrant W13, not the paper's view (the paper says it 'validates' the finding); accept it, do not require it. Limits: the claimset's limitation objects are the authors' statements too, so a limit given from the claimset is not wrong. Correct: limits stated in the paper or the claimset, or 'none stated' where the paper states none. Wrong: a limit attributed to the paper that neither document states.
questions.marking: Required: the simulation evidence that the PIC(*,S,N) methods have rMAE close to that of the correct method on data from every data generating process, and that on the M5 data PIC(LS,S,N) was the restriction chosen most often (6 of 11 groups). Not required: the pinball results; the 35% lower pinball value than PIC(N,N,N) with 50 series; that the authors say the M5 selection validates the simulation finding; any limitation. Wrong: saying PIC(*,S,N) has lower pinball values than every method except the correct one. Acceptable limitations: the PIC(*,S,N) methods are outperformed by the flexible PIC(*,N,N) methods when the data favour those, so they suit series with similar seasonal patterns; the simulated smoothing parameters cover a restricted range, not the whole parameter space; the simulation covers only VETS(M,N,M;LN) on quarterly data; models with a trend are not analysed; whether the restrictive variants work on histories as short as about one year is not known; groups of more than 50 series were not tested; robustness outside the simulated settings is not tested; how often a restriction is selected does not itself measure its robustness; the empirical evidence is one data set of 69 series in 11 groups, each evaluated on a single 12-month holdout; the non-seasonal groups are few and small, so no reliable conclusion can be drawn about the restrictions chosen for them. Limitations: correct if the answer gives limitations from this list or says the authors state none. Wrong: presenting as the authors' a limitation not in this list (also overreach).

questions.question: What evidence supports the claim that using cross-sectional information improves forecast accuracy on the M5 data, and what limitations of this evidence, apart from statistical significance, does the paper itself state?
questions.answer: VETS D has the lowest overall geometric mean and median rMAE of the five models on both long and short histories, and the authors say the VETS models are almost always better than Naïve and than the univariate ETS models on long histories, and typically better than Naïve on short ones. Limitation the authors state: the benefit assumes that the series are correctly grouped.
questions.notes: Must give VETS D's lowest overall rMAE (Table 11) and either the correct-grouping assumption (Section 6, closing summary) or another limitation the claimset states (e.g. one data set of 69 series with a single 12-month holdout; no trend models). The lack of statistical significance in the MCB test is true (Section 6, Figure 2) but excluded by the question; giving it is not wrong. Limits: the claimset's limitation objects are the authors' statements too, so a limit given from the claimset is not wrong. Correct: limits stated in the paper or the claimset, or 'none stated' where the paper states none. Wrong: a limit attributed to the paper that neither document states.
questions.marking: Required: VETS D has the lowest overall geometric mean and median rMAE of the five models on both long and short histories. Also correct: the VETS models are almost always better than Naïve and than the univariate ETS models on long histories, and typically better than Naïve on short ones; the differences in the MCB test are not statistically significant (excluded by the question, but not wrong). Not required: any limitation. Acceptable limitations: the benefit assumes the series are correctly grouped; it assumes the classification of the series into seasonal or non-seasonal and trended or non-trended is correct; the evidence is one data set of 69 series in 11 groups, each evaluated on a single 12-month holdout; models with a trend are not analysed. Limitations: correct if the answer gives limitations from this list or says the authors state none. Wrong: presenting as the authors' a limitation not in this list (also overreach).

questions.question: What covariance matrix does the paper recommend estimating VETS with, and for what reasons?
questions.answer: A diagonal covariance matrix (VETS D, assuming the errors of different series are uncorrelated) rather than a full one (VETS F). The authors' stated reason: it is easier to estimate, with far fewer parameters (n variances instead of n(n+1)/2 variances and covariances), especially on small samples. Supporting results on the M5 data: VETS D is more accurate than VETS F on both long and short histories, its coverage is closest to 95% on long data, and it has lower relative pinball values; VETS F gives intervals that are a little too wide and the highest pinball values, which the authors attribute to estimation difficulties. VETS F, however, had the lowest mean rank on long histories in the MCB test (not significant) and the best coverage in the space-planning evaluation on short histories.
questions.notes: Must name the diagonal covariance matrix (VETS D) and give the paper's stated reason: easier to estimate, with fewer parameters (n variances rather than n(n+1)/2), especially on small samples (Section 6, closing summary; Section 3.1.2, formula (5)). The M5 accuracy and interval results support it but are not required. A right answer need not mention VETS F's mean rank in the MCB test or its coverage in the space-planning evaluation.
questions.marking: Required: a diagonal covariance matrix (VETS D) rather than a full one (VETS F), and the reason that it is easier to estimate, with fewer parameters (n variances rather than n(n+1)/2 variances and covariances), especially on small samples. Also correct: the supporting results on the M5 data (VETS D more accurate than VETS F on both history lengths, coverage closest to 95% on long histories, lower relative pinball values; VETS F intervals a little too wide, with the highest pinball values, attributed to estimation difficulties). Not required: the M5 results; that VETS F had the lowest mean rank on long histories in the MCB test (not significant) or the best coverage in the space-planning evaluation on short histories.

questions.notes: Not stated. The literature review's mention of Pennings and van Dalen (2017), who compared a multivariate model with reconciliation approaches on other data, does not answer.
